newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bonds rally on CPI quickly tires.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds rally on CPI quickly tires.

text.p: FUTURES CASH YIELD
*The Australian 10-year bond yield struck a fresh 3-1/2 year low on inflation report but quickly ran into profit-taking as the rally showed signs of flagging.
*Costello again says last rate cut yet to impact.

The Australian 10-year bond yield struck a fresh 3-1/2 year low as second quarter inflation came in just below median expectations, but quickly ran into profit-taking as the rally showed signs of flagging.
"The bond market rally is close to reaching exhaustion," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

The benchmark October 2007 bond yield neared 6.40 percent after news headline inflation in the second quarter fell 0.2 percent for an annual rate of 0.3 percent. The policy sensitive underlying rate rose 0.3 percent for 1.7 percent annually, its lowest since the series started in 1971.

The data fuelled expectations of another easing in monetary policy, although with a 50 basis point reduction in current official 5.5 percent interest rates largely factored in, the market is finding it difficult taking the rally much further.
"We are close to seeing the all-time low in the 10-year part of the curve. Certainly the short-end has very little value left in it," Citibank's Koukoulas added.
"We are probably only going to see one more rate cut occur on the back of the low inflation performance," he added.
September bill futures struck a high of 94.96 on the data, equating to a cash rate of 5.04 percent.
The 10-year bond futures contract hit a high of 93.595 at one stage, but failed to push ahead to the all-time high of 93.630 set in early 1994.

Like bonds, bill futures also failed to hold the highs with the market still needing to see Thursday's average weekly ordinary time earning before it is fully confident that a policy easing is on the agenda.

Treasurer Peter Costello also cast some doubt on the timing of an easing, again saying that the last rate cut on May 23 had yet to fully flow through to the business community, and that rate policy is focussed on 12-18 months ahead.

The market had gone into the data extremely bullish, not only on the expected outcome of the data, but also on the back of a strong rally in U.S. Treasuries following comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.

In his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, Greenspan said that U.S. growth was slowing for the time being, heading off the need for now to raise interest rates. He was also confident that U.S. inflation would be modest in 1997.
The U.S. Treasury market rallied strongly in New York on Greenspan, which saw the price of the U.S. 30-year bond jump over 1-1/2 points, and the advance continued in Tokyo.

The failure to push on the rally on an extremely positive inflation outcome saw yield spreads to the dollar bloc widen out. Analysts at Colonial State Bank pointed out Australia's 0.3 percent annual headline inflation compares with 1.5 percent in Canada, 1.1 percent in N.Z. and 2.2 percent in the U.S.
